## What is confirmed

An agent's ticket writes were **lost** and survived only because it also described them in its
prose report. Specifically, on `torrential-unwhite-snail` (`9c2e-b44c-119e-4105`) the agent:

- retitled the ticket and raised it to priority 2, and
- posted a root-cause comment containing a fully reproduced diagnosis (the four-xdist-workers /
  four-gate-slots exhaustion, with a serial-vs-parallel experiment).

Neither reached the shared store. Verified directly afterwards: the ticket was still **priority 3
with 1 comment**, its original state. The finding was recoverable only because I could re-derive it
from the agent's report text and re-verify its three load-bearing facts against `origin/main`
myself.

That is a data-loss path through the shared record. The next agent to hit it may not restate its
findings in prose, and then the work is simply gone.

## The reported mechanism — RELAYED, and NOT currently reproducible

The agent reported that its worktree's ticket-store clone had diverged from `origin/tickets` with
**no shared history**, `rebar fsck` saying *"The local store was built independently of the remote
... its writes will never push"*, and **2,492 unpushed commits across 142 distinct tickets**.

I could not reproduce this. Checking three agent worktrees minutes later:

    fix-acli-ceiling-partition        in sync      <- the very worktree that reported divergence
    bug-9c93-ad8d-user-data-mounts    in sync
    fix-b2ff-mcp-readonly-empty       ahead/behind (shared history, normal)

and the shared store on the main checkout was `local HEAD == origin/tickets`, with `rebar fsck`
reporting **no divergence line at all**. So the condition was transient and had healed by the time
I looked. The 2,492/142 figures are the agent's measurement, not mine, and I am recording them as
relayed rather than established.

## The one thing that worked, worth preserving

The failure was **loud at the end**: the agent's final two writes were REFUSED, with `fsck` naming
the condition and the remedy. That is why the agent noticed at all. Whatever the fix, keep that —
a silent local-only accumulation would be far worse than a refusal.

But note the asymmetry that produced the loss: writes made BEFORE the refusal appeared to succeed
locally and were stranded silently. Only the last two were refused. So "loud on refusal" is not the
same as "loud on divergence".

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Reproduce the divergence deliberately in a scratch worktree, or establish that it cannot
      recur and say why. This ticket rests on a relayed observation; the first job is to make it
      first-hand or refute it. A refutation is a valid outcome — close it as `not_a_bug` with the
      evidence.
- [x] Determine whether a worktree created by `make worktree` gets its own tracker clone, and
      whether that clone can be built independently of the remote (the `fsck` text and the
      `ENV_ID_MISMATCH` note both point at a re-clone that did not carry `.env-id` /
      `.opcert-key` / `.ensure-applied`).
- [x] A store that CANNOT push is detected at the first write, not the last. Proven by driving a
      write against a deliberately-diverged clone and observing the refusal on write #1.
- [x] If stranded commits are recoverable, the recovery path is documented and does not require an
      operator to reconstruct findings from an agent's prose. `rebar fsck-recover` exists but is
      mutating; establish whether it preserves stranded events or discards them, because those are
      very different remedies when 142 tickets' worth of another session's work is involved.
- [x] The interaction with concurrent sessions is stated: this host runs eleven worktrees against
      one shared `tickets` branch, and any recovery that rewrites shared history is unsafe while
      others are writing.
